title: On mechanistically accessible copolymer sequences
authors: Richard Golnik, Nicola Vassena, Alex Blokhuis
abstract: Structural observations in polymer chemistry are often rationalized through underlying mechanistic insights. The study of families of mechanisms - and the phenomenology and lawlike behavior that can accompany them - is less common. Here we construct a theory that links a mechanistic feature - the number of nearest neighbors $k$ that influence monomer incorporation - with the accessible copolymer sequence space.   We find that the reaction mechanisms can be mapped 1-to-1 to a regular de Bruijn graph of degree $k$. We calculate the periodic copolymer sequences as function of neighbor index $k$, and number of monomers $s$. We show that the number of periodic sequences grows explosively with $s,k$, bounded from below by $s!^{s^{k-1}}/s^k$. We find that periodic k-polymerization is governed by several simple laws describing allowed sequences, number of specific reactions, repeating unit length and the allowed and disallowed sequence coexistence in block copolymers.   We formulate Simple Assembly Rules (SAR) that capture commonly observed behavior and design of literature systems, and characterize the possible k-polymerizations they are allowed to access ($k\leq2$) as function of symmetries and illustrate our findings with reported examples from the coordination chemistry and supramolecular chemistry literature.   We discuss chemical-structural contributions by which nontrivial ($k>1$) sequences are formed, highlighting the importance steric hindrance, long-range interactions and degrees of freedom.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to map the chemical mechanism of copolymerization to the mathematical structure of a de Bruijn graph. It quantifies the accessible sequence space based on the number of influencing neighbors ($k$) and monomer types ($s$). By introducing Simple Assembly Rules (SAR), the authors characterize sequence formation, while also identifying the necessity of long-range interactions to achieve the full theoretical sequence potential.
main_problem: To construct a theory linking the mechanistic feature—the number of nearest neighbors ($k$) influencing monomer incorporation—to the accessible copolymer sequence space.
main_result: The mechanism maps 1-to-1 to a regular de Bruijn graph, and the number of periodic sequences grows explosively with $s$ and $k$. Simple Assembly Rules (SAR) capture much of the observed behavior, but long-range interactions are needed to access all possible sequences.
method: The authors use graph theory (de Bruijn graphs) to model polymerization, deriving sequence constraints through concepts like the single-repeat law and formulating Simple Assembly Rules (SAR) based on local interactions.
model_or_system: The system is $k$-polymerization, where monomer addition depends on the last $k$ incorporated monomers (vicinality $k$). The process is modeled using Markov processes and analyzed via the structure of the resulting de Bruijn graph.
key_observables: The number of periodic sequences ($\gamma(s, k)$), the number of distinct block types ($	heta$), and the structure of the transition matrix ($\partial$).
important_parameters: Neighbor index ($k$), number of monomer types ($s$), and the length of the sequence ($s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the mechanism to a de Bruijn graph and formulating SARs, which are shown to be limited in scope without considering long-range interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $k$-copolymerization for small $s$ and $k$, showing de Bruijn graphs and elementary circuits. Tables summarize the count of periodic sequences $\gamma(s, k)$ and map sequence types to SAR indices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the graph-theoretic mapping of $k$-polymerization to calculating the number of periodic sequences. It then introduces and analyzes the Simple Assembly Rules (SAR) framework, culminating in discussions on how long-range interactions are required to extend the accessible sequence space beyond SAR constraints.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework linking local chemical rules (mechanisms) to global sequence space constraints is highly relevant to understanding complex, non-equilibrium assembly processes in soft matter and supramolecular chemistry, which share mathematical parallels with open quantum systems dynamics.
